content.text: The City of Washington From the Serial Set Tap to read full story By Elina LeeDigital Resources Division, Law Library of CongressThe U. S. Congressional Serial Set, commonly referred to as the Serial Set, contains House and Senate Documents, House and Senate Reports, Senate Executive Documents and Senate Executive Reports bound by the session of Congress. Documents cover a wide variety of topics and history. Publication of the Serial Set began with the 15th Congress, 1st Session (1817). The Law Library of Congress and the Government Publishing Office (GPO) are collaborating to digitize Serial Set documents published between the 15th (1817) and 103rd (1994) Congresses (See Serial Set timeline (e)). These are important historical resources that include not only legal and committee reports related to bills and foreign affairs, but also geographical information. Serial Set citations are noted in [brackets] and cited in the sources section.Note: (e) refers to an external-facing link. The City of Washington Washington, D.C. was founded on July 16, 1790. Washington, D.C. is a unique and historical place among American cities because it was completely planned for the national capital and needed to be distinct from the states. President George Washington chose the specific site (e) along the Potomac and Anacostia Rivers. The Serial Set contains a lot of information about the plan for the city of Washington, including maps, bills, and illustrations. In this Story Map, you can see original plans and pictures of Washington, D.C. The Plan for the City of Washington "Washington has an advantage over the modern cities of the world, with possibly the one exception of St. Petersburg, in having been designed and laid out as the capital city of a great nation. Congress, after much discussion, located the Federal City on the Potomac River by act of Congress, which was approved by President Washington July 16, 1790." [²]The first map of Washington was authorized by an act of Congress in July, 1790 (H. Doc. no. 240 at 37 (1932), reprinted in Serial Set Vol. No. 14909). As the initial phase in preparing the map, Peter Charles L'Enfant wrote to Jefferson April 4, 1791, requesting maps and data concerning London, Madrid, Paris, Amsterdam, Naples, Venice, and Florence. Streets, parks, and the sites for the President's House and the Capitol are all shown on the map made by L'Enfant in 1791 essentially as they exist today. "By the plan of the city of Washington, in the territory of Columbia, the Capitol in that city is intended as a first meridian for the United States of America" [³]The plans were related to the establishment of Washington as the nation's capital and they showed Georgetown, the President's House, the Capitol, the National Mall, and more. The Serial Set also describes how Washington, D.C. streets were named.“We have agreed that the federal district shall be called ‘the Territory of Columbia’ and the federal city ‘the city of Washington,’ (commissioners’ letter-book No. 16, page 32, September 9, 1791). The title of the map will therefore be a map of the city of Washington in the Territory of Columbia....We have also agreed the streets be named alphabetically one way and numerically the other, the former divided into north and south, letters, the latter into east and west, numbers, from the Capitol.” [⁴] Map of Present City of Washington Public Buildings and Grounds The Serial Set describes plans of government buildings, including contracts, contingent expenses, and reports of the commissioner of public buildings. History of the U.S. Capitol The U.S. Capitol (e) is among the most symbolically important and architecturally beautiful buildings in the nation. Its design competition was suggested by Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson and President George Washington, with an award of $500. The first winner was Dr. William Thornton and the second winner was Stephen H. Hallet. Because Thornton was inexperienced with building technology, the construction was initially supervised by Stephen Hallet. However, he modified a lot of Thornton's plans and was quickly replaced by George Hadfield and James Hoban. [²] The U.S. Capitol., Bell & Bro., [Between 1860 and 1930], Prints and Photographs Division. (Stereograph of Capitol building on left; written description of building authored by Bell & Bro. on right). "The Capitol fronts the east, and stands on a plateau ninety feet above the level of the Potomac, in latitude 38° 53' 20".4 north and longitude 77° 00' 35".7 west from Greenwich. It was constructed of sandstone, painted white, from an island in Aquia Creek, Virginia." [⁴] Construction of the U.S. Capitol began in 1793. It has been constructed, burned, reconstructed, extended, and restored over the course of its nearly 230-year history. You can watch a short video, The History of the United States Capitol (e), created by the Architect of the Capitol (e). Washington Monument The Washington Monument (e) is also a symbolic structure. It was designed by Robert Mills and completed by Thomas Casey and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. The structure was completed in two phases of construction due to the budget and the Civil War, one private (1848-1854) and one public (1876-1884). As a result, the stone color couldn't be matched and the structure has two slightly different shades. The Library of Congress The Library of Congress is the largest library in the world. The original Library of Congress was established in 1800, but was destroyed in 1814 during the War of 1812. The following year, it was replenished by Congress with the purchase of the library belonging former President Jefferson, encompassing about 7,000 volumes.Unfortunately, it was destroyed by fire again in 1851. It was rebuilt in 1852 when $75,000 was fitted up with ornamental iron cases and iron ceilings, fireproof building materials. [⁵] Government Printing Office (GPO) The United States Government Publishing Office (e), formerly the United States Government Printing Office, is a federal agency created by Congress in June 1860. The U.S. Government Printing Office started operations on March 4, 1861 with 350 employees. The Serial Set contains information about many other topics related to the City of Washington. For more updates, follow the From the Serial Set series on In Custodia Legis, the Law Library of Congress blog.U.S. Congressional Serial Set References[¹] H.
